  The Network's Mental Health Module Library includes a collection of evidence-informed learning modules designed to support mental health literacy among post-secondary students across Canada. All module content has been compiled "for students, by students," with relevant Subject Matter Experts providing a thorough review for validity and psychological safety.

    Module 1
    Introduction to Mental Health
    Released April 2022
    In this introductory module, you will learn how mental health and mental illness are distinct, but interconnected concepts. You will learn about the basic fundamentals of mental health, including important terms and concepts, risk factors for the development of mental illness, delivery of mental health care in Canada, and different levels and barriers to help-seeking. Throughout the module, we'll emphasize real-world application of these ideas and concepts to the post-secondary student context.
  

  
  
    Module 2
    Mental Health and Stigma
    Released June 2022
    In this module, you will learn about the different types of stigma, as well as the broader impact that stigma can have on individuals living with mental illnesses. Generally, stigma is a negative connotation associated with a circumstance or quality. Stigma is not only an issue due to its effects on the mental health of individuals living with a mental illness, but is also considered to be one of the greatest barriers to the development of mental health programs and help-seeking worldwide. 
  


  
    Module 3
    Mental Health and Intersectionality
    Released May 2022
    This module examines intersectionality, a framework for understanding how overlapping identities, such as race, gender, disability, and sexuality, interact with systems of privilege and oppression. It explores the experiences of marginalized communities, including BIPOC, Indigenous, disabled, and 2SLGBTQIA+ populations, and the barriers they may face. The module also looks at how these intersections can impact mental health and well-being, considering factors like socioeconomic status, education, and systemic discrimination.

    Social risk factors for the development of mental illness or mental health deterioration can include:
    
    
      Lack of social support and/or isolation from others

      Low socioeconomic status

      Neurological deficits or injuries

    Psychological risk factors for the development of mental illness or mental health deterioration can include:

      Self-depreciation
      Certain personality traits, thoughts, emotions, and attitudes

    Our physical and mental health are closely related - taking care of ourselves physically can help us to maintain good mental health.

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
1.1 Defining Stigma
Stigma concerning mental health can be difficult to define. Watch this TedTalk to gain an introduction to what stigma is, and how we can reduce the stigma surrounding mental illness.

Stigma in the Context of Mental Health
Stigma is one of the major barriers to accessing mental health treatment. It can impede social interaction, lower quality of life, interfere with social roles, and prevent timely access to treatment (Centre for Addictions and Mental Health, n.d.). This creates a cycle of disadvantage. Recently, anti-stigma efforts have increased in many countries, including many taking place in Canada.

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
1.2. Types of Stigma
There are many different types of stigma including public, or social, structural, and self-stigma. Some also consider there to be a fourth type: stigma-by-association. Click through the grid below to learn the basic definitions of each.




  
    
      
        
          
          Public Stigma
        
        
          Public Stigma
          The typical definition of stigma which highlights the views of the public towards mental health issues or a specific condition.
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Self-Stigma
        
        
          Self-Stigma
          Occurs when an individual internalizes the negative stereotypes associated with their illness.
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Structural Stigma
        
        
          Structural Stigma
          In the context of mental illness, structural stigma refers to the rules, policies, and practices of social institutions that arbitrarily restrict the rights of, and opportunities for, people with mental illnesses.
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Stigma-by-Association
        
        
          Stigma-by-Association
          Involves stigma towards an individual based on their associations with stigmatized persons (i.e., someone experiencing a mental illness).
        
      
    
    click to flip
  




1.2.1 Public Stigma
Public stigma is what most people think of when they say “stigma”. Public stigma highlights the views of the public towards mental illness or a specific condition.

Includes public stereotypes and prejudicial attitudes toward people with mental illness
Stems from a history of considering those suffering from mental illness to be “mad and to”taint” the family, since it was considered hereditary

This type of stigma can pose serious, negative implications to individuals struggling with their mental health. For example, a public stigma surrounding mental illness is that people with mental illness are dangerous, incompetent, unstable and may even be the one to blame for their disorder. Though this seems like just an idea, these public stereotypes can have serious consequences on the lives of people living with mental illnesses, and are the basis for many discriminatory practices.
As a result of these stereotypes, discrimination may take place in the form of employers refusing to hire individuals living with a mental illness, landlords refusing to rent to them, and even healthcare systems offering lower standards of care.
Examples of Public Stigma
Let’s check out some examples of public stigma experiences.




  
    Stigma in Healthcare Settings
    Stigma from Friends and Family
  

  
    
    
      Stigma in Healthcare Settings
      Mental healthcare providers are said to contribute largely to public stigma through their behaviours towards patients seeking help. 
      Individuals who seek services from mental health professionals often rate these providers as being among the most stigmatizing groups they encounter.
      Among reports include being patronized, excluded from decisions on treatment, assumed to lack the capacity to be responsible for their lives, told their hope for recovery is limited, and told they will never work in regular careers, complete school, or even be a parent.
      
    
  

  
    
    
      Stigma from Friends and Family
      Friends and family are also reported sources of public stigma towards individuals living with mental illnesses. 

      Individuals with lived experience of mental illness report friends and family members views towards their loved one appeared to change upon the discovery of their mental illness. The majority of this change is often the result of social stigma. Friends and family may experience shame and/or fear that a scandal would occur if others find out that they are friends with/related to someone with a mental illness.

Typically, the more severe the illness, the stronger these feelings are. Additionally,  feelings of embarrassment and shame are often accentuated in cases where the mental illness in question is addiction or substance use.

    
  

  
    ←
    1 / 2
    →
  







1.2.2 Self-Stigma
Self-stigma occurs when an individual internalizes the negative stereotypes associated with their mental illness. This means they begin to believe the negative social conceptions held by society surrounding their condition. Individuals experiencing a mental illness report experiencing stigma as even more limiting and devastating to their lives than their illness. The negative consequences of self-stigma are far reaching, including reductions in self-esteem and self-efficacy, leading to more negative thoughts and in some cases, even suicidal ideation.

Self-stigma occurs when an individual living with a mental illness has thoughts such as, “I am incompetent and incapable and it’s my fault I’m not getting better.”

Labeling Theory
Labeling theory is a perspective that goes hand-in-hand with self-stigma and has been proposed as an explanation for its occurrence. Labeling theory states that diagnosing an individual with mental illness places a label upon them and they feel they are associated with any societal implications of being mentally ill, such as being incapable or dangerous. Eventually, the feelings of bearing the burden of society’s negative stigma lead to an individual attempting different defensive behaviours to prevent society’s rejection and further judgement. These defensive behaviours may include hiding their treatment or withdrawing from it as well as disengaging in social interactions. These result in more unfortunate circumstances such as higher unemployment rates and reduced social relationships.


1.2.3 Structural Stigma
Structural stigma occurs in the context of mental health when laws, policies, and practices of institutions result in unfair treatment of those with mental illness. While it often occurs unknowingly (through implicit cognitive biases), it expresses the inequities embedded in the fabric of our social institutions, organizations, and our shared ways of thinking and acting. It is further manifested through cycles of blame, shame and mistrust for individuals who seek help for their mental illness or addiction.
Finding a way
This type of stigma is especially harmful to those with lived experience of mental illness. It can result in inequitable access (including housing, employment, etc.) and a lower quality of healthcare for these individuals, whether their concerns are related to physical health, mental health, and/or substance use.

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
1.3. Consequences of Stigma
Stigma can have consequences at both the individual and societal levels, including but not limited to: 1) barriers to treatment, 2) unemployment, and 3) intersectional consequences.

1.3.1 Barriers to Treatment
Despite recent advancements in reducing the stigma surrounding common mental health challenges like anxiety and depression, barriers to treatment remain. Below, we’ve organized these into barriers that individuals living with mental illness may face before, during, and after receiving a diagnosis and/or treatment.


  
    Before
    During
    After
  

  
     The stigma surrounding mental illness is one reason that people may find it extremely difficult to reach out and seek treatment. Seeking treatment is a step which requires overcoming the daunting thought of condemning oneself to being labelled as “mentally ill”.
  

  
     During treatment, patients may experience the stigma from mental health providers through their behaviour toward them. Patients are often treated by the mental health providers in ways that coincide with the stigma surrounding individuals with a mental illness (such as treating patients as if they cannot be responsible for their own lives and speaking to them differently than others without a mental illness).
  

  
     Due to both external and self-stigma, individuals may hide that they are receiving treatment and reduce themselves from social interactions to avoid additional rejection. It is a struggle for people suffering from mental illness to continue their treatments as the stigma surrounding it often results in the desire to hide and withdraw from treatments altogether.
  





 TedTalk: Stop the Stigma
In this video, Heather Sarkis speaks about why it is important to openly talk about mental health and mental illness.



1.3.2 Unemployment
Most people with mental illnesses or mental health concerns are willing and able to work, but are often unable to due to factors outside their control.
In 2017, Statistics Canada found that of people surveyed with a mental health-related disability, less than half (46%) were employed. This demonstrates a significant unemployment rate for individuals living with a mental illness. Furthermore, more than half of the people surveyed who reported living with a mental illness believed they were disadvantaged in terms of employment due to the stigma surrounding their condition.
The stigma of mental illness causing unemployment results in detrimental consequences. Employment provides not only income and financial stability but also daily routine and structure, social interactions, a sense of achievement and purpose, and a sense of identity.



  
    "The deprivation of benefits to employment alone are enough to cause suffering in previously mentally healthy individuals, and the suffering is magnified for those with a mental illness."
  


  
    Social Stigma and Unemployment - BMC Psychology
    Social stigma is an underestimated contributing factor to unemployment in people with mental illness or mental health issues: position paper and future directions.
  
  Learn More



1.3.3 Intersectional Consequences
Issues related to stigmatization are multiplied for people who are additionally stigmatized for other reasons, including race, gender, sexuality, and more. For more information on mental health and the stigma surrounding marginalized groups, we recommend you check out our module on Mental Health and Intersectionality.


  1.4 Section Summary
  
    Stigma is a major barrier to accessing mental health treatment for those who might be in need of it.
    Stigma can take many forms, including public stigma, self-stigma, structural stigma, and stigma-by-association.
    The consquences of stigma are far reaching, including stigma itself serving as a barrier to treatment / help-seeking, unemployment, as well as intersectional consequences for those who are additionally stignatied for other characteristics.

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
2.1 Stigmatizing Language 
Sometimes individuals unknowingly contribute to the stigmatization of mental illness in subtle ways. Such ways may include using derogatory terms and/or phrases in conversation. There are many stigmatizing phrases and terms used that are often used without the realization that they are contributing to the stigma around mental illness.

The language we use every day matters, and it is important to be sensitive to those living with mental illnesses. Common stigmatizing words or phrases to avoid include: “That made me wanna kill myself”, “I’m so bipolar”, or “My boss is really OCD.”

Many common phrases - like those depicted above - demean mental illnesses and contribute to the overall stigmatization of them in society. Though they are common phrases and may appear harmless on the surface, their common use increases both public stigma in society as well as the self-stigma a person living with a mental illness may internalize.
A person with lived experience of mental illness may hear comments like these and reflect more negatively on themselves, or choose not to reach out to their support network as a result of feeling that people view their illness as a joke. These seemingly harmless words can “downplay” serious illnesses, and are insensitive to those who live with mental illnesses day in and day out.

  
    Combat Mental Health Stigma with Language Shifts
    This resource from the Mental Health Commission of Canada discusses ways to reduce stigma in our conversations.
  
  Learn More

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
2.2 Mental Health Literacy
For any hope to eradicate mental health stigma, steps must be taken to address stigma on several levels. This includes addressing it at the level of specific individuals, their social interactions with others, and on the large-scale level of society. One way to do this is by improving mental health literacy.



  
    Improving our mental health literacy helps us become responsible, effective, and successful in living full and healthy lives, as well as in supporting our friends and family.
  

What is Mental Health Literacy?
Overall, the development of mental health literacy (MHL) came from health literacy, which was informed by the universal and concrete observation that low functional literacy in regard to any form of health is associated with endless poor health outcomes. MHL was originally conceptualized as “knowledge and beliefs about mental disorders which aid their recognition, management, or prevention” (Kutcher et al., 2016). It was then refined to include knowledge that benefits the mental health of others and it became important to also focus on the health promotion aspect of MHL.
Over years of evolving and refining definitions, this eventually led to the most recent definition of MHL: “understanding how to obtain and maintain positive mental health; understanding mental disorders and their treatments; decreasing stigma related to mental disorders; and, enhancing help-seeking efficacy” (Kutcher et al., 2016).

  
    Learn more about Mental Health Literacy
    Visit mentalhealthliteracy.org to learn more and to access toolkits and resources related to mental health literacy.
  
  Learn More



  
    Previous definition
    "Knowledge and beliefs about mental disorders which aid their recognition, management, or prevention."
    Jorm et al. (1997)
  

  
    →
  

  
    
      Updated definition
      "Understanding how to obtain and maintain positive mental health, understanding mental disorders and their treatments, decreasing stigma related to mental disorders, and enhancing help-seeking efficacy."
    
    (Kutcher et al. 2016)
  


Good mental health literacy in young people and their key helpers may lead to better outcomes for those with mental disorders, either by facilitating early help-seeking by young people themselves, or by helping adults to identify early signs of mental disorders and seek help on their behalf.


  
    
  
  
    
  


Mental Health Literacy and Stigma
Most research on the subject shows that mental health literacy does not directly combat stigma when you consider the stigma that exist due to existing prejudices and discrimination. Often, people ignore available information that contradicts their existing beliefs. Instead, mental health literacy aims at correcting misconceptions with factual information.

  1
  A primary way to intervene early by implementing MHL within schools. This can be done through a third-party organization, or through the school’s teaching staff after they have been educated on the content themselves. Many studies have shown a significant improvement in overall mental health knowledge and help-seeking behaviour.



  2
  MHL can also be implemented in other aspects of life, such as informational campaigns, in the workplace (such as within new employee training, company-funded MHL seminars, etc.), and at home. At home, parents should become well-versed with MHL in order to educate their children and have conversations within the home about mental health.

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
2.3 Mental Health Education 
Educational approaches to ending stigma present facts about the condition with the aim to correct any misinformation or contradicting negative attitudes or beliefs. There are a mass number of stereotypes and misconceptions regarding mental illness/disorder and can vary in content and severity based on the specific type of mental illness/disorder.
Stereotypes
Stereotypes are incredibly harmful to both the person dealing with mental health issues as well as the people who are supporting them. Stereotypes often stem from misunderstanding and fear, but can generate a large number of issues for others (Oexle et al., 2018). Explore some examples of the negative impact of stereotypes below.




  
    
      
        
          
          Not Seeking Help
        
        
          Not Seeking Help
           Not seeking help due to fear of being judged, losing their job, or internal feelings of inadequacy/blame. 
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Loss of Hope
        
        
          Loss of Hope
          Reduced hope of recovery or improvement and reduced likelihood of sticking with treatment, possibly due to stereotypes such as “people with mental illness will never fully get better” or “people with mental illness are to blame for their struggles”.
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Fear of Judgement
        
        
          Fear of Judgement
          Difficulty in social situations or sharing comfortably about mental health problems due to fear of judgment, fear, or misunderstanding. 42% of Canadians were unsure whether they would socialize with a friend who has a mental illness (Mental Illness and Addiction, n.d.). 
        
      
    
    click to flip
  
  
  
    
      
        
          
          Bullying
        
        
          Bullying
          Increased bullying and/or physical harassment or violence from others due to stereotypes stemming from misunderstanding and fear.
        
      
    
    click to flip
  



Debunking Stereotypes
Many stereotypes can be “debunked” (exposed and unlearned) through an educational approach. Using the information you have learned so far, try to debunk the following stereotypes.


  
    
       Myth #1: Mental health problems are not as severe as physical ones.
      +
    
    
      Truth: Major depressive disorder is understood to be the second leading cause of disability worldwide (Lozano et al., 2012). The disease burden of mental health and addiction is actually 1.5 times higher than all types of cancers put together in Ontario (Mental Illness and Addiction, n.d.). About 4000 Canadians die per year from suicide (Mental Illness and Addiction, n.d.). Statistics like these show the urgency of mental illness and how it should be taken just as seriously as any other deathly physiological issue or disease.
    
  

  
    
      Myth #2: People with severe mental health problems are scary or dangerous to society.
      +
    
    
      Truth: People with mental health problems are actually at higher risk for being attacked or hurting themselves than hurting other people (Stigma and Discrimination, 2015). Stereotypes actually cause an increase in bullying and/or physical harassment and harm (Oexle et al., 2018). People fear what they do not understand, so without evident and productive mental health education and literacy, misunderstandings and fear are produced.
    
  

  
    
      Myth #3: People who struggle with depression are lazy.
      +
    
    
      Truth: Within the diagnostic requirements for major depressive disorder, some of the main symptoms are extreme and constant fatigue, diminished interest in most or all things, and a diminished ability to think and/or concentrate. The change in someone’s productiveness or activity levels is not laziness, but a symptom(s) of the disorder.
    
  

  
    
      Myth #4: Struggling with mental illness and/or seeking help means you are weak.
      +
    
    
      Truth: Seeking help for mental illness should be looked at as the same as seeking treatment for any other health condition or disorder. It in no way shows weakness or flaws in yourself. If anything, it shows strength..
    
  


TedTalk: Overcoming Mental Health Stereotypes Overcoming mental health stigma and stereotypes is difficult. The TedTalk below shares one woman’s story of doing just that.

title: Mental Health and Stigma
text:
2.4 Other Ways to Reduce Stigma
It is important to target the behavioural outcomes of the stigmatization process (discrimination and social inequity), which is consistent with rights-based or social justice models that emphasize social and economic equity for those with disabilities (such as equitable access to services, education, work etc.). For example, it is important to create alliances with researchers and program evaluators in order to critically evaluate anti-stigma activities and build better, evidence-based practices.
In this section, we will learn about 3 different types of interventions designed to reduce stigma: 1) awareness-raising, 2) contact-based, and 3) peer advocacy and services.




  
    Awareness-Raising
    Contact-Based
    Peer Advocacy/Services
  

  
    
    
      Awareness-Raising Interventions
      This type of intervention is typically a multi-factored approach and occurs during a specific period in time. Often, awareness-raising interventions are organized by an organization or group of organizations.

The goal of this type of initiative is to raise awareness and open a dialogue on mental health and illness. Unfortunately, these types of programs are often not evaluated, so it is difficult to know what kind of effect they have and whether their objectives were met.


  
    World Mental Health Day
    The World Health Organization has designated October 10 as World Mental Health Day. All stakeholders working in mental health are encouraged to talk openly about their work, to raise awareness of mental health concerns around the globe, and to discuss ways to improve mental healthcare access.
  
  Learn More

      
    
  

  
    
    
      Contact-Based Interventions
      Across a wide range of stigmatizing conditions, people without the stigmatized conditions have little meaningful contact with those who have these conditions. Lack of contact fosters discomfort, distrust, and fear. Contact-based anti-stigma campaigns are one way to foster connection and facilitate positive interactions.

Contact-based education involves people with lived experience of mental illness educating students by sharing their personal stories with positive recovery messages. Contact-based anti-stigma campaigns have been shown to reduce stigma at the individual level. This type of intervention can raise awareness and correct misconceptions, though there is mixed evidence regarding its ability to change behaviours and maintain change long-term. As a result, contact-based education does not often reduce stigma at the macro- or structural-level.

  
  
However, the value of contact-based anti-stigma education at the individual level should not be dismissed. For adolescents and emerging adults, fostering connection in an online setting may be beneficial and appealing. The internet is often able to provide anonymity which is preferred by patients (especially when first seeking a connection). In general, the effects of contact in person are higher than those by video or online, but some still prefer the online option.

Contact-based campaigns are often combined with educational and mental health literacy initiatives. This involves information being presented, and then people with lived experience supporting and personalizing the information by relating it to their own life experiences. Although combined interventions generally show an advantage over educational interventions alone, they are implemented less often.
      
    
  
 
  
    
    
      Peer Advocacy/Services
      These interventions are based on the same concept as contact-based campaigns: that social connection and positive interactions can contribute to reducing stigma.

Peer service providers are people with lived experience who work as health care team members and foster the provision of nonjudgmental, non-discriminatory services while openly identifying their own experiences. An example is the grassroots organization Active Minds, a college student mental health advocacy group based in the United States (see the video below for more info). Peer support also aims to counterbalance discrimination, rejection and isolation individuals may feel when seeking mental health support or treatment. 


  
  

      
    
  





  2.5 Section Summary
  
    There are many types of stigma related to mental illness: public stigma, self-stigma, structural stigma, and stigma-by-association. Public stigma is the typical definition of stigma, which highlights the views of the public towards mental health issues or a specific condition. Self-stigma occurs when an individual internalizes the negative stereotypes associated with their illness. Structural stigma is introduced by large, societal structures (e.g., laws, policies, practices that result in unfair treatment). Stigma-by-association occurs when an indiviudal is stigamtized as a result of their elationship with a member of a stigmatized group (e.g., indidviudals living with mental illnesses).
    Stigma can have many harms and societal consequences, including: the formation of serious barriers to help seeking and recieving proper diagnoses and treatment; unemployment resutling in lack of income and financial stability, as well as daily routines/structure and sense of purpose; and intersectional impacts for those who are stigmatized for other reasons, such as race, gender, or sexuality.
    Many types of anti-stigma interventions were introduced in this module, including: mental health education, mental health literacy, awareness-raising campaigns, contact-based interventions, and peer advocacy/services.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
1.1 What is Mental Health?
The terms mental health and mental illness are often used interchangeably, but this is incorrect. Everyone has mental health - whether it is good (“flourishing”) or bad (“languishing”), but not everyone lives with a mental illness. In this section, you’ll learn how to distinguish between these two distinct terms, and understand how they are inextricably linked.
Mental health is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as “a state of well-being in which an individual realizes his or her own potential, can cope with the normal stressors of life, can work productively, and can make a contribution to his or her community.”
Mental illness implies that a person has received a clinical diagnosis and/or is experiencing clinically significant symptoms of mental illness. Mental illnesses envelop a broad categorization of conditions and can be short-lasting episodes or chronic, lifelong disorders.

Having a mental illness isn’t inherently “bad” and having symptoms of a mental illness isn’t either. It comes down to what “being healthy” and “recovery” means to each individual.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
1.2 Who can diagnose mental illnesses?
In Canada, the following professionals can diagnose mental illness:

Family Physicians
Family physicians are medical doctors primarily trained in family medicine. Family doctors can prescribe medications and may be able to refer or connect you with a provider of psychotherapy.
Psychologists
Psychologists hold a master’s and/or doctoral degree in psychology and often further specialize in specific areas of mental health. Psychologists specialize in providing psychotherapy.
Psychiatrists
Psychiatrists are medical doctors who go on to specialize in mental health and mental disorders. Psychologists can provide pharmacotherapy (prescribe medications) and psychotherapy.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
1.3 When are mental illnesses diagnosed?
The timing of developing a mental illness varies based on a number of factors (including biopsychosocial risk factors and the mental illness in question), but research suggests that 75% of mental illnesses occur before the age of 25 (Kessler et al. 2007).
Given that the average age for post-secondary students ranges from 18-25 - a period also referred to as emerging adulthood (Arnett 2000) - students are considered to be a particularly “at risk” group for mental health deterioration. Notably, post-secondary institutions are reporting that more incoming undergraduate students are arriving at school with pre-existing mental illnesses. In fact, recent research suggests that rates of mental illnesses in the post-secondary population are not significantly different from those found among the general Canadian population (Wiens et al. 2020).






Note



That’s not to say that working towards improving mental health among post-secondary students is unnecessary - quite the opposite. These reports suggest that students are in need of tools and education to help build their resiliency in the face of a myriad of stressors faced over the course of their post-secondary education. We hope that Canada’s Student Mental Health Network can provide some of this support to students.





  
    "Mental illness will affect all Canadians at some point in their life, either directly or indirectly (through a friend, family member, or acquaintance)."
    – Canadian Mental Health Association

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
1.4 Why is mental health important?
As you’ve learned, we all have mental health, and the effects of poor mental health and mental illness can be wide-reaching. The Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA) reports the following mental health-related statistics(opens in a new tab):

Approximately 1 in 5 individuals will experience a mental illness each year.
50% of Canadians have experienced, or will experience a mental illness by the age of 40
Mental illness will affect all Canadians at some point in their lifetime, either directly or indirectly (through a friend, family member, or acquaintance).

Mental ill health has a significant economic impact, too. The burden of mental illnesses to the Canadian economy was estimated to be $51 billion in 2003 (Lim et al., 2008), with more recent projections estimating the total cumulative costs over the next 30 years will exceed $2.5 trillion (Smetanin et al., 2011). This reflects both direct costs (i.e., healthcare) and indirect costs (i.e., loss of employee productivity, short- and long-term disability claims). In 2012, CMHA reported that approximately one fifth (21.4%) of the working Canadian population experienced either poor mental health or a mental illness, negatively impacting their productivity.


  1.5 Section Summary
  
    Mental health and mental illness are distinct, but interconnected. Everyone has mental health. Not everyone has a mental illness.
    Mental illnesses can be diagnosed by family doctors, psychiatrists, or psychologists. Each care provider can provide different treatment options (medication, therapy, or both).
    The majority of mental illnesses have their onset during adolescence, and emerging adults (aged 18-25) are at increased risk.
    The impact of mental health is wide-reaching, both with respect to the proportion of Canadians it effects and its economic impact.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
section: 2.1 Connecting Mental Health and Mental Illness
text:
2.1 Connecting Mental Health and Mental Illness
While mental health and mental illness are distinct concepts, they are inextricably connected. In his groundbreaking 2002 paper, Corey Keyes established the Dual Continuum of Mental Health and Mental Illness. Since its publication, the Dual Continuum has been widely adopted by subject matter experts and practitioners around the world studying mental health or providing mental health care.
This model conceptualizes mental health and mental illness as separate, but interconnected continuums. Mental health can range from good (or “flourishing”) to poor (or “languishing”), sitting anywhere along that spectrum. Our mental health moves flexibly along this continuum from day to day, month to month, etc. Similarly, an individual can move along the mental illness continuum, ranging from no mental illness to severe mental illness. Importantly, the severity of a mental illness can be influenced by frequency, longevity, and severity of individual symptoms, in addition to the degree to which the illness is being managed.

Importantly, it is possible for an individual to experience good mental health (or to “flourish”) while living with a well-managed mental illness. Similarly, it is possible for an individual to experience poor mental health without meeting the clinical threshold for a mental illness. In the best-case scenario, we would find ourselves in the upper right-hand quadrant of the Dual Continuum model, with good mental health and no mental illness. In the worst case scenario, someone “in crisis” might find themselves in the bottom left-hand quadrant of the model, with poor mental health and severe mental illness.






Note



Remember: It isn’t inherently “bad” to live with a mental illness. Many people live with well-managed, lifelong mental illnesses (such as chronic anxiety, or even more complex mental illnesses like bipolar disorder) and still experience “flourishing” mental health.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
2.2 Lived Experience Examples
Let’s check out some examples of young adults who have shared their lived experience with mental illness and/or fluctuating mental health.




  
    Gisela
    Alicia
  

  
    
    
      Living with Anxiety and Depression — and Flourishing
      Gisela is a lawyer, and a Black Dog Institute volunteer (a medical research institute in Australia). In her story, Gisela shares that she has experienced feelings of anxiety since high school, which worsened once she started university. Gisela was diagnosed with depression at 21.
      "I felt very guilty for being unwell because my life was objectively very good [...] I've learned that you don't have to justify having depression."
      With support from her friends, Gisela reached out for help, and now lives with well-managed anxiety and depression thanks to cognitive therapy techniques and a toolkit of breathing exercises. Gisela also finds that talking to people about her experiences is both meaningful and helpful in maintaining the flourishing mental health she now has.
      Read Gisela's original post ↗
    
  

  
    
    
      Taking Care of my Mental Health during the COVID-19 Pandemic
      Alicia Raimundo is a Kids Help Phone National Ambassador and a mental health advocate. Like many of us, Alicia's mental health took a hit during the COVID-19 pandemic as a result of the uncertainties and social isolation.
      "It's been very helpful for me to remember and explore what I can do, instead of focusing on what I can't do."
      In her story, Alicia shares five methods she used to cope with these changes and feelings over the course of the pandemic, including allowing herself to grieve and setting aside time for self-care and connection with family and friends.
      Read Alicia's original post ↗

  2.3 Section Summary
  
    Everyone has mental health, but not everyone lives with a mental illness.
    Living with a mental illness is not inherently "bad" - in fact, it is possible to live with a well-managed mental illness and experience good mental health.
    Our mental health is flexible and can fluctuate from day to day and week to week based on a number of different factors; you'll learn more about this in the next section.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
3.1 What Affects your Mental Health?
Mental health is complex, and can be affected by social, psychological, and biological factors. Certain aspects can place individuals at increased risk for experiencing deterioration in their mental health and/or the development of a mental illness. Fluctuations in our mental health are common and normal, and almost never stem from a sole reason.


  
    Social
    Biological
    Psychological
  

  
    Social risk factors for the development of mental illness or mental health deterioration can include:
    
      Lack of social support and/or isolation from others
      Abusive relationships
      Weak social safety net (family and community factors)
      Low socioeconomic status
      Exposure to discrimination
    
  

  
    Biological risk factors for the development of mental illness or mental health deterioration can include:
    
      Genetic vulnerability
      Health comorbidities (or generally poor physical health)
      Poor nutrition or sleep patterns
      Neurological deficits or injuries
      Substance abuse
    
  

  
    Psychological risk factors for the development of mental illness or mental health deterioration can include:
    
      Prolonged exposure to stress
      Traumatic experience(s)
      Dissatisfaction with current life status
      Self-depreciation
      Certain personality traits, thoughts, emotions, and attitudes

title: Introduction to Mental Health
section: 3.2 The Link Between Physical and Mental Health
text:
3.2 The Link Between Physical and Mental Health
Physical and mental health are interdependent on one another. There are a multitude of physical factors that can influence your mental health, but we will focus below on the following three: diet, physical activity, and sleep.



  
    
    
      Diet
      What we decide to eat and drink can have a significant influence on the development, management, and prevention of mental illness and mental health deterioration. Evidence suggests that nutrition is a protective factor against depression and anxiety, while an unhealthy diet acts as a risk factor (Lim et al. 2016).
      A healthy diet is defined by sufficient macro (carbohydrates, fats, and protein) and micronutrient (vitamins and minerals) consumption. See Canada's Food Guide for more detail on achieving and maintaining a healthy diet.
    
  
  

  
    
    
      Physical Activity
      Staying physically active not only keeps you physically healthy, but mentally healthy too (Tyson et al. 2010). Evidence suggests that endorphins released during exercise result in positive mental health effects. As little as 10 minutes of physical exercise can have a positive effect on energy, mood, and mental alertness, though adults should aim to get 150 mins of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per week. Check out Canada's Physical Activity Guidelines for more information.
      No time to get to the gym? Remember that exercise can also be: walking, doing household chores, raking leaves or shovelling snow, etc. There are also online resources that can help you exercise outside of the gym (Nike Training Club App, Yoga with Adriene).
    
  
  

  
    
    
      Sleep
      We get that achieving the recommended 7–9 hours of sleep every night isn't always possible. However, it's important to note that lack of sleep increases the risk of mental health deterioration and the development of some mental illnesses. Lack of sleep can also cause heightened stress and irritability, while good quality sleep has been found to improve mental health and overall well-being (Scott et al. 2021).
      On the flip side, mood and mental health can drastically affect sleep quality. Individuals with anxiety or heightened levels of stress tend to have more issues with sleep, making this a bit of a double edged sword. Resources for improving your sleep are provided by the Mayo Clinic and CMHA BC/Anxiety Canada.
    
  




  3.3 Section Summary
  
    Social, biological, and psychological factors can increase our risk of developing a mental illness or experiencing mental health deterioration.
    Some of these factors may be out of our control (i.e., genetic vulnerabilities), while others are very much within our control (i.e., nutrition, physical activity, and sleep quality).
    Our physical and mental health are closely related - taking care of ourselves physically can help us to maintain good mental health.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
4.1 Mental Health Care in Canada
Healthcare in Canada is governed by the Canada Health Act, with the goals of promoting and restoring the mental and physical health of Canadians and to ensure reasonable access to health services, regardless of factors like income, education, or culture. Provinces and territories are provided with funding from the federal government to provide coverage for health services deemed to be “medically necessary” (Canadian Civil Liberties Association 2017).
Unfortunately, the majority of mental health services are not considered “medically necessary” - psychological services are paid for out-of-pocket or covered by insurance, producing substantial barriers for many Canadians who are in need of mental health care. We’ll take a closer look at barriers to help-seeking in the next section. While mental illness accounts for approximately 10% of the burden of disease in Ontario, it receives just 7% of health care dollars (CAMH, 2022).
Since its inception in 2007, the Mental Health Commission of Canada has taken strides to improve mental health care in Canada, releasing (Changing Directions, Changing Lives) in 2012 - Canada’s first mental health strategy. The strategy highlights a number of strategic priorities, including promotion and prevention, recovery and rights, access to services, disparities and diversity, Indigenous mental health, and leadership and collaboration.

Mental health has long been recognized as a fundamental aspect of one’s health, however under our current health regime, the majority of mental health services do not meet the eligibility requirement of “medically necessary.”

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
4.2 Mental Health Care Providers
Earlier in this module, we explored three mental health care providers who can formally diagnose mental illnesses: family doctors, psychologists, and psychiatrists. A family doctor can provide you with a referral to a psychiatrist, and may be able to recommend a psychologist to you (though a referral is not required).
Each of these care providers is qualified to offer different types of treatment. Family doctors can prescribe medication, but do not typically provide psychotherapy. Psychologists specialize in providing psychotherapy, but cannot prescribe medication. Psychiatrists can prescribe medication and offer psychotherapy. It’s common to work with more than one care provider on your mental health.
It’s important to note that not everyone struggling with mental health deterioration will require medication and/or psychotherapy in order to recovery. In fact, many people - and especially those who have not yet hit the threshold for a mental illness diagnosis - may benefit from lower-intensity options.






Note



Note that post-secondary students can access both physical and mental health services from their Student Wellness Services (SWS) on campus. You don’t need to wait until the next time you’re home to see your family doctor. The practitioners at your SWS will be happy to work with your family doctor back home to put together a treatment plan that works best for you.





  
    "Not everyone requires medication and/or therapy to recover from a mental illness or languishing mental health. Some may excel with just one or the other, while others may benefit from even lower intensity care."

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
4.3 The Mental Health Service Continuum
The Mental Health Service Continuum, shown below, describes the different levels of mental health care. As you can see, there is a relationship shown between the level of need (e.g., the severity of one’s mental health deterioration or mental illness) and the intensity of care provided.
The Mental Health Services Continuum is comprehensive, in that it shows services ranging from upstream to downstream. Upstream services are those that aim to intervene prior to the development of symptoms, while downstream services are intended for intervention following the development of symptoms (and diagnosis).
Ordered from upstream to downstream, the levels of mental health services described below include: mental health promotion, mental illness prevention, early detection, treatment, and recovery.



  

    
    
    
    

    INTENSITY OF CARE
    LEVEL OF NEED

    Low
    High
    Low
    High

    
    ← UPSTREAM
    DOWNSTREAM →

    
    
    
    

    
    RECOVERY

    PROMOTION
    
      
    

    PREVENTION
    
      
    

    EARLY
    DETECTION
    
      
    

    TREATMENT
    
      
    

  

  
    
    
  



In Canada, we tend towards the “medical model” or “treatment model” when it comes to mental health - in other words, we focus on treating the symptoms of mental illness or poor mental health, and not the cause. Along with other experts in the field, the Mental Health Commission of Canada recommends that we work towards adopting a more comprehensive, holistic view of mental health care, placing emphasis on upstream services (i.e., mental health promotion and mental illness prevention). In doing so, we can work towards preventing the development of mental illness to begin with, thereby alleviating bottlenecking at the treatment level, which produces long wait times and other accessibility challenges.


  4.4 Section Summary
  
    Health care in Canada is covered by the Canada Health Act, though many mental health related services do not qualify for funding under the current definition of "medically necessary".
    Not everyone struggling with mental health deterioration may require formal medical treatment - there are many different types of mental health care along the service continuum.
    Mental health promotion and mental illness prevention are upstream interventions that occur before the development of symptoms of mental illness.
    Early detection straddles upstream and downstream, aiming to intervene as soon as possible after the development of initial symptoms, while treatment and recovery are more firmly downstream services that aim to treat and manage mental illness.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
5.1 Reaching out for Help
So far in this module, we’ve learned that mental health problems are widespread, affecting a large proportion of Canadians. However, national data suggests that a large proportion of Canadians with a demonstrated need for mental health care do not reach out for help or treatment. Similar patterns of low levels of help seeking have been observed among Canadian post-secondary students. But why?
When you’re experiencing mental health deterioration, it can be really difficult to reach out for help. The longer you wait to reach out for help, the more severe your symptoms can become, making even more difficult to contact your doctor, or even get out of bed.



  
    "Of the 2.3 million Canadians who reported unmet or partially met mental healthcare needs in 2018, the most frequently reported barriers were not knowing where to get help, being too busy, or not being able to pay for services (Moroz et al. 2020)."

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
5.2 Help-Seeking by the Numbers
Data from the Canadian Community Health Survey (Statistics Canada, 2019) demonstrates the following:

Almost one-in-five Canadians needed mental health care in 2018, and half of them felt that their needs were fully met.
In terms of the type of care needed, the need for medication was the most likely to be met (85.4%) while the need for counselling was the most likely to be unmet (34.1%).
The most frequently reported reasons for having unmet or partially met needs were related to not knowing where to go, being too busy or not being able to afford to pay.

title: Introduction to Mental Health
text:
5.3 Barriers to Help Seeking
Three of the most common barriers to seeking help for mental health related issues in Canada are accessibility, affordability, and stigma. Click through the grid below to learn a bit more about each.




  
    
      
        
          
          Accessibility
        
        
          Accessibility
           Issues of accessibility can include a lack of available care providers, a lack of appropriate care providers (i.e., culturally competent care, care providers that specialize in a specific mental illness), lack of available transportation to services, and long wait times. 
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Affordability
        
        
          Affordability
          Mental health services are most often paid out-of-pocket or covered by insurance, presenting a substantial financial barrier to many, particularly the unemployed or those employed in positions that do not include benefit plans.
        
      
    
    click to flip
  

  
    
      
        
          
          Stigma
        
        
          Stigma
          In the context of mental health, individuals with mental illnesses often fear that they will be stigmatized or discriminated against as a result. Self-stigma, where an individual internalizes this stigma, can also be a barrier to seeking help. 
        
      
    
    click to flip
  




While accessibility, affordability, and stigma are often talked about, they stem from much larger, structural barriers to reaching out for help. In the same way that social inequality and disadvantage lead to disparities in mental health outcomes, they also lead to inequities related help-seeking. The barriers faced by individuals operate within three main levels: the individual level, the community level, and the system level. Explore the tabs below to learn more.
For an excellent, more detailed breakdown of the barriers to accessing mental health care in Canada, we recommend (Moroz et al.’s 2020 paper).


  
    Individual-Level Barriers
    Community-Level Barriers
    System-Level Barriers
  

  
    Individual-level barriers can include:
    
      Impact of the symptoms of mental illness
      Side effects of medication
      Episodic nature of mental illness
      Educational disadvantage
      Self-stigma
      Logistical (i.e., financial burden, unaccommodating work schedule, transportation)
    
  

  
    Community-level barriers can include:
    
      Community and workplace stigma
      Low expectations for healthcare professionals
      Lack of culturally appropriate care
      Language barriers (i.e., care not provided in language other than English)
    
  

  
    System-level barriers can include:
    
      Disincentives caused by the income support system
      Lack of intersectoral collaboration between mental health and employment services
      Lack of available services due to client saturation and/or limited practitioners
      Lack of timely care (i.e., long wait times for care)
    
  






  5.4 Section Summary
  
    Many Canadians with a demonstrated need for mental health care do not reach out for help or treatment, and the same can be said of post-secondary populations.
    Three major barriers to help-seeking include accessibility, affordability, and stigma. Visible minorities tend to experience some of these barriers more than others. 
    Barriers to help-seeking operate at three main levels: individual (i.e., self-stigma, side effects of medication), community (i.e., lack of culturally appropriate care, language barriers, perceived stigma), and system (i.e., lack of available practitioners, lack of timely care).
